docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Know every device on your home network, what changed, and what needs you — without sending anything to the cloud.

Lanxang (formerly Atlas) is a self-hosted watchdog for homelabs. It finds every machine on your LAN without installing anything on them, maps how they are cabled together down to the switch port, watches your Docker containers and Proxmox guests, checks your network's security, and alerts you when something new shows up or something important goes quiet. An AI model is optional: run one locally with Ollama and ask questions in plain language.

Watch everything. Change nothing without asking.

Lanxang observes and explains. Restarting a container or a VM is only ever suggested, and every action asks you first. There is no autonomous mode and no bypass flag.

docs.title: What Lanxang does
docs.text:
• Device inventory: every device on the LAN, found from ARP, SNMP and LLDP. New ones wait for you to name them; important ones alert you when they drop off.
  • Cabling map: a wired view from the internet down to every switch port — link speeds, PoE, spanning tree, link bundles, VLANs and your patch panels — read over SNMP and (optionally) your UniFi console.
  • Security watch: new open ports on LAN devices, a rogue DHCP server, ARP spoofing of your gateway, expiring TLS certificates, what reaches the internet and what the internet can reach, and whether your torrent client is still behind its VPN.
  • Health: cable errors, temperatures near their limit, full disks, crashed or restart-looping containers.
  • Alerts where you already look: ntfy, Discord, Slack, email, any webhook, Signal, or 100+ services through Apprise. One alert when a problem starts, one when it clears.
  • Containers and VMs: Docker, Proxmox and libvirt — what's running, what's unhealthy, and restart, stop or resize when you approve it.
  • Chat with your homelab (optional): answers come from live state, logs and your own notes, using Ollama on your own hardware or Claude.

Start with Getting Started, or see Architecture for how the pieces fit together.

docs.title: Where this is headed
docs.text: Lanxang isn't meant to run on your laptop and poke at infrastructure from the outside — see Deployment for the intended model of Lanxang running as a guest on the Proxmox host it's helping you manage. The Roadmap covers what's shipped and what's next.

docs.title: CLI Reference
docs.text: All 35 current Lanxang commands. Run lanxang <command> --help for any command-specific options.

docs.title: Status & health
docs.text: Command Description lanxang version Display the Lanxang version. lanxang status Display current Lanxang status. lanxang init Interactively generate lanxang.yaml — prompts only for Proxmox/AI provider/Prometheus settings, skips whatever you decline, never writes ANTHROPIC_API_KEY to disk. Logs the session to logs/lanxang-init-<timestamp>.log (secrets redacted) for troubleshooting and records. Optional — Lanxang runs on safe defaults without an lanxang.yaml at all. lanxang doctor Run Lanxang health checks (Python, memory, storage, Docker, inventory, other virtualization/orchestration backends detected on the host) plus live reachability checks for the optional integrations you've configured (Proxmox, AI provider — Anthropic stays config-only to avoid a billed call, Ollama is checked live — Prometheus), each bounded by a short timeout so a dead endpoint can't hang the run. --json prints {"checks": [...], "healthy": bool} instead. Exits 1 if any check is unhealthy, in either output mode - safe to check $? from cron without --json. lanxang config Display the active Lanxang configuration. lanxang runtime Display Lanxang runtime information.

docs.title: Discovery & reporting
docs.text: Command Description lanxang discover Discover infrastructure information — built-in (system, hardware, storage, network) and every registered plugin — in one pass, and generate inventory. lanxang report Generate an infrastructure report from the latest inventory. --json prints the raw inventory dict instead of writing reports/atlas-report.md - null if lanxang discover hasn't run yet. No exit-code logic, same as lanxang trends. lanxang docker Display Docker container status. lanxang services Detect known homelab services running in Docker (see Service Catalog). lanxang compose Analyze a Docker Compose file. lanxang map Build the network map shown at lanxang web's /map — an interactive graph (Cytoscape.js, vendored and served locally, so it works offline) drawn from the device inventory plus this snapshot. Hosts in a row with their guests and Docker networks inside, other devices in a grid, most important first. Internet → LAN → machines, with this host's containers grouped by Docker network and their public hostnames (Traefik), Proxmox guests, libvirt guests, each map.hosts entry's TCP reachability, the AI endpoint, and what Lanxang may act on. Colours: green=seen, amber=quiet, red=important+quiet, grey=never seen; dashed border=new (needs triage). Click a device to edit (name/kind/state/tags/notes/important flag) or link to the full device page (merge/split). Double-click a host to fold/unfold its guests. "Show ignored" checkbox filters the view. Without JavaScript, falls back to a static SVG map. Saved as a snapshot (GET /api/graph[?ignored=1] returns the data); --json prints it. Run it on a schedule to keep the map current. lanxang scan Find every device on the LAN (TCP-connect to port 9 on every address so the kernel ARP-resolves it, then read /proc/net/arp) and update the device inventory - links each sighting to a known device when certain, queues new devices for triage, and sends Signal alerts for new devices and important devices gone quiet (requires scan.enabled: true, see Configuration). --json prints the scan result. Exits 1 on scan failure, recorded as a failed source run rather than making devices look quiet. Run by the atlas-scan container. lanxang devices List the device inventory: every device Lanxang knows, its status (seen / quiet / invisible), IP, state, and which sources have sighted it. --json prints the full inventory, including each device's individual sightings. lanxang proxmox scan Scan Proxmox infrastructure — nodes, VMs, and containers — and report what changed since the last scan (requires proxmox.enabled: true, see Configuration). lanxang monitor Query Prometheus for host metrics and flag any at or above their configured threshold (requires monitoring.enabled: true, see Configuration). --json prints the full scan as one payload instead. Exits 1 if disabled=false and Prometheus is unreachable, or if any metric exceeded its threshold; exits 0 when disabled (an intentional state, not a failure) - in either output mode. lanxang trends Show host, per-container, and per-Proxmox-guest resource-usage trends (latest/min/max/avg) from the environment snapshots lanxang monitor/lanxang proxmox scan have been saving. --limit controls how many recent snapshots to consider (default 20). --json prints {"host": {...}, "containers": {...}, "guests": {...}} instead - no exit-code logic, since a trend report has no health/threshold concept to signal. Guest memory_percent is percent of the guest's own allocated memory, not host-relative like container memory_percent is.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text: Command Description lanxang plugins Display registered Lanxang plugins. Running their discovery is folded into lanxang discover (see above).

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
Commands that change infrastructure rather than just observe it. All are approval-gated — see Architecture.

Command Description lanxang restart <name> Restart a Docker container. --node <fleet-node> retargets the connection to that node's Docker daemon over SSH (docker-py's ssh:// transport) instead of the local one - same confirmation, same event path, just a different client. Shows the container's current state and asks for confirmation before acting. lanxang stop <name> Stop a Docker container without removing it. --node <fleet-node> supported, same as lanxang restart. Shows the container's current state and asks for confirmation before acting. lanxang resize <name> Resize a Docker container's CPU (--cpus <cores>) and/or memory (--memory <limit>, e.g. 512m/1g) limit, live, without a restart. --node <fleet-node> supported, same as lanxang restart. Shows the container's current configured limit(s) and asks for confirmation before acting. lanxang proxmox restart <vmid> Restart a Proxmox VM or LXC guest. Shows the guest's current state and asks for confirmation before acting (requires proxmox.enabled: true and write/power-management permission on the token, see Configuration). lanxang proxmox stop <vmid> Shut down a Proxmox VM or LXC guest via an ACPI request (not a hard power-off) - may not complete if the guest OS isn't responding. Shows current state and asks for confirmation. lanxang proxmox resize <vmid> Resize a Proxmox guest's CPU (--cpus <cores>, maps to Proxmox's cpulimit) and/or memory (--memory <limit>) limit. For a qemu guest, may need hotplug enabled to apply without a restart; LXC applies live. Asks for confirmation. lanxang libvirt restart <name> Restart a libvirt/KVM guest via an ACPI virsh reboot request - like Proxmox's stop, may not complete if the guest OS isn't responding. --node <fleet-node> retargets virsh at that node via its native -c qemu+ssh:// transport - no new dependency. Shows current state and asks for confirmation. lanxang libvirt stop <name> Stop a libvirt/KVM guest via an ACPI virsh shutdown request (not virsh destroy, libvirt's hard power-off) - same no-force-fallback caveat as restart. --node <fleet-node> supported, same as lanxang libvirt restart. Shows current state and asks for confirmation. lanxang libvirt resize <name> Resize a libvirt/KVM guest's vCPU count (--vcpus <count>, an integer - a different concept from Docker/Proxmox's fractional --cpus limit) and/or memory (--memory <size>, e.g. 512MiB). Applies at next boot only - a running guest needs hotplug already configured to pick this up live, not attempted here. --node <fleet-node> supported, same as lanxang libvirt restart. CLI-only: not wired into lanxang analyze/lanxang chat's suggestable actions. Asks for confirmation.

docs.title: Knowledge & AI
docs.text: Command Description lanxang history Display recorded operational events. lanxang intelligence Display the latest stored environment context. lanxang analyze Analyze the latest environment snapshot with AI — using live tool calls for current state — and print a summary plus recommendations (see Configuration). --json prints {"summary", "recommendations", "plan", "provider", "model"} instead - never offers to run a suggested plan (no bypass flag), that's text-mode-only. No environment yet prints null, exit 0. Exits 1 on an AIProviderError, otherwise 0 - the one JSON-output command in this project with a real exit code for something other than reachability, since analysis has a genuine health concept report/trends don't. lanxang chat Interactive multi-turn chat with Lanxang about your infrastructure. No prior lanxang discover required — grounds itself against live state on demand. Type exit to quit. lanxang web Serve a local web view (overview/triage/devices/interactive map/coverage/history/trends) over the same data lanxang report/lanxang history/lanxang trends already read, plus a device inventory editor. /map is an interactive graph (Cytoscape.js, vendored locally, offline-capable) of machines, containers, and guests with colour-coded status, editable side panel, and fold controls; click a device's name for "Ask lanxang about this device" link. /chat is the same assistant as lanxang chat — read-only tools, suggested actions, and multi-step plans with per-step Approve buttons; steps are re-grounded before execution and recorded in history. --host/--port (defaults 127.0.0.1:8420). The /devices/<id> edit page and /api/devices/<id> POST (plus merge/split), /api/graph (map data), /api/chat, and /api/actions/execute are same-origin-gated, and every page needs sign-in (lanxang's own admin password, or web.auth: proxy behind Authelia and similar). Runs in the foreground until Ctrl+C, same on-demand shape as every other command. lanxang auth password / setup-code / token [--new] Sign-in for lanxang web: set or reset the admin password (signs everyone out), print the first-run setup code, print (or replace) the read-only API token dashboards send as Authorization: Bearer <token>. lanxang notify test Send a test alert to every channel under notify: (ntfy, webhooks, email, Apprise, Signal) and show which got it. Exits 1 if any failed or none is set. lanxang ports check Open-port watch (see Configuration): common service ports on online LAN devices, this host's listeners, router port forwards / UPnP. The first run learns; later runs alert once per newly open port. --json prints the saved state. lanxang certs check Certificate watch (see Configuration): expiry date of every public hostname's TLS certificate (Traefik routes plus security.cert_hosts). Checks once a day unless --force; alerts at 14 and 3 days left, on an untrusted certificate, and when renewed. --json prints the saved state. lanxang internet check Internet view (see Configuration), opt-in with posture.internet_view: asks Shodan's InternetDB what it last saw on the home's public IP. Checks once a day (or when the public IP changes) unless --force; alerts once per open port not in posture.expected_ports and per reported CVE, and when it clears. A failed lookup keeps the last answer and is retried an hour later. --json prints the saved state. lanxang internet speed Speed test, opt-in with internet.speed_test (see Configuration): download, upload and ping against speed.cloudflare.com, about 260 MB. Runs once a day after 04:00 in notify.timezone; --force runs one now. Shown on Home. lanxang lan check Rogue DHCP servers and gateway ARP spoofing (see Configuration): one DHCP discover that never takes an address, plus the gateway's MAC from the ARP table. Saves the result for the Security tab (Exposure) and alerts once per new problem. --trust-gateway accepts the gateway's current MAC after a router swap; --json prints the result. Exits 1 while a problem is open. Needs host networking (atlas-scan runs it). lanxang fleet doctor SSH into every node under fleet.nodes in lanxang.yaml (no config = "no fleet nodes configured", exit 0) and run lanxang doctor --json on each, reusing that same payload rather than a fleet-specific format. -o BatchMode=yes fails an auth prompt fast instead of hanging the whole scan; a per-node SSH/parse failure is reported as "reachable": false without aborting the rest. --json prints {"nodes": [...], "healthy": bool}. Exits 1 if any node is unreachable or unhealthy - safe to check $? from cron. No remote actions and no persistence - a live fan-out per invocation, not a saved snapshot. lanxang fleet trends SSH into every fleet node and run lanxang trends --limit <n> --json on each, reusing that payload. --limit (default 20) passed through per node. No fleet-wide health concept (same as lanxang trends) - --json prints {"nodes": [...]}, exit 1 iff any node is unreachable. lanxang fleet report SSH into every fleet node and run lanxang report --json on each, reusing that payload. A reachable node with no inventory yet reports {"reachable": true, "inventory": null}, distinct from an unreachable one - not a parse failure. No fleet-wide health concept (same as lanxang report) - --json prints {"nodes": [...]}, exit 1 iff any node is unreachable.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Settings live in lanxang.yaml next to docker-compose.yml, and secrets in .env. Environment variables use the LANXANG_ prefix. Coming from Atlas, see Upgrading from atlas.

Lanxang uses YAML configuration, loaded from lanxang.yaml in the current working directory. If the file doesn't exist, Lanxang runs on defaults (safe — no Proxmox connection is attempted, discovery is fully enabled, no AI model is used until you choose one).

Prefer a web page? The Setup tab sets up alerts (ntfy, webhooks, email), the AI model, managed switches (SNMPv3), a UniFi console and Proxmox, with a Test button for each. Tests are read-only: alerts send one test message, switches get one SNMP request, UniFi and Proxmox are signed in to and read. It saves to inventory/settings.yaml and keeps passwords in inventory/secrets.json (readable only by lanxang), both in the data volume. Anything you set in lanxang.yaml or .env wins and shows read-only there. Until alerts are on and every device has a name, the Home page shows a short Getting started list linking to each step.

Run lanxang init to generate this file interactively instead of writing it by hand — it only prompts for the fields below that actually vary per deployment (Proxmox, AI provider, Prometheus), leaves discovery/inventory at their defaults, and logs the session to logs/ for troubleshooting. The reference below is for editing the result by hand, or understanding what each field does.

name: homelab

discovery:
  hardware: true
  storage: true
  network: true

inventory:
  directory: inventory/generated

proxmox:
  enabled: true
  host: 192.168.1.10
  user: atlas@pve
  token_name: atlas-token
  token_value: ""
  # password: ""
  verify_ssl: false

intelligence:
  provider: anthropic
  model: claude-opus-5
  ollama_host: http://localhost:11434

monitoring:
  enabled: false
  prometheus_url: http://localhost:9090

fleet:
  nodes:
    - name: media-server
      host: 192.168.1.20
      user: lanxang
      port: 22
      identity_file: ""

docs.title: name
docs.text: A label for this Lanxang instance. Defaults to atlas-node.

docs.title: discovery
docs.text:
Toggles which discovery categories lanxang discover collects. All default to true.

Field Default Description hardware true CPU and memory information storage true Disk partitions and usage network true Hostname and network addresses

docs.title: inventory
docs.text: Field Default Description directory inventory/generated Where lanxang discover writes system-inventory.yaml

docs.title: proxmox
docs.text:
See Deployment for why a scoped API token is preferred over the account password.

Field Default Description enabled false Must be true for lanxang proxmox scan to attempt a connection host "" Proxmox host/IP user "" Proxmox user, e.g. atlas@pve token_name "" API token name — preferred over password token_value "" API token value password "" Fallback if not using a token verify_ssl false Verify the Proxmox host's TLS certificate

If both a token and a password are configured, the token is used.

Read access (the built-in PVEAuditor role) is enough for lanxang proxmox scan. lanxang proxmox restart <vmid> needs additional power-management permission on top of that — confirmed against a real Proxmox instance, granting the built-in PVEVMUser role (which includes VM.PowerMgmt) at path / is enough. If the token has Privilege Separation enabled (Proxmox's default), that permission has to be granted to the token identity itself (user@realm!tokenid), not just the user — see Deployment for the exact gotcha and fix.

docs.title: intelligence
docs.text:
Controls the AI backend behind lanxang analyze.

Field Default Description provider none none, ollama or anthropic model claude-opus-5 The Claude model ID, or an Ollama model name (e.g. llama3.1) when provider: ollama ollama_host http://localhost:11434 Only used when provider: ollama think false Only used when provider: ollama. Thinking models such as qwen3 reason silently before answering, which is much slower — false keeps replies fast. Set null if your Ollama or model rejects the field.

Chat's read-only tools: get_containers, get_services, get_recent_events, get_last_analysis, get_container_logs, get_posture, get_devices (filter: all/new/quiet, at most 40), get_alerts, get_disks, get_uptime, plus get_internet_view when posture.internet_view is on. Lists are capped with a more count; a tool whose data isn't set up answers not set up with where to turn it on.

The Anthropic provider reads its API key from the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable — it is never stored in lanxang.yaml.

docs.title: monitoring
docs.text:
Controls lanxang monitor.

Field Default Description enabled false Must be true for lanxang monitor to attempt a connection prometheus_url http://localhost:9090 Base URL of an existing Prometheus server cpu_threshold 90.0 CPU usage percentage at or above which lanxang monitor flags the metric memory_threshold 90.0 Memory usage percentage at or above which lanxang monitor flags the metric disk_threshold 90.0 Disk usage percentage at or above which lanxang monitor flags the metric

The default metric queries assume node_exporter is running on the monitored host and being scraped by Prometheus — install and configure it there for lanxang monitor to return real CPU/memory/disk figures. If Prometheus is reachable but node_exporter isn't set up yet, lanxang monitor still runs; each affected metric just reports as unavailable rather than failing the whole command.

A metric at or above its threshold prints with a yellow ! instead of a green ✓ (e.g. ! cpu_percent: 92.1% (threshold: 90.0%)), and if anything crossed its threshold, lanxang monitor publishes atlas.monitoring.threshold_exceeded (visible via lanxang history) alongside the atlas.monitoring.scan.completed event every scan already publishes — so a no-op scan doesn't add event-log noise, only an actual threshold crossing does. A metric with no data (node_exporter not scraped, etc.) is never flagged either way — "unavailable" isn't "under the limit."

docs.title: fleet
docs.text:
Controls lanxang fleet doctor. No daemon, no central server — each node just needs to be reachable over SSH with Lanxang already installed there; lanxang fleet doctor SSHes in and runs lanxang doctor --json remotely.

nodes is a list, each entry:

Field Default Description name (required) A label for this node, shown in lanxang fleet doctor's output host (required) Hostname or IP to SSH to user lanxang SSH user port 22 SSH port identity_file "" Path to an SSH private key; empty uses your normal SSH agent/default key

An empty nodes list (the default) means "no fleet nodes configured" — lanxang fleet doctor exits 0, the same way a disabled Proxmox/monitoring integration does, not an error state.

docs.title: knowledge
docs.text:
Your own notes, for lanxang chat.

Field Default Description notes_paths [] Folders (or files) of Markdown, text and scripts (.sh, .py, .yml, unit files...) to search. Empty = no search_notes tool. Hidden folders (.git) are skipped. pinned_paths [] Short files (a host/IP map, conventions) attached to every chat question. Keep them small. auto_context 3 How many best-matching note sections are attached to every question automatically (0 = only when the model calls search_notes).

Markdown is searched section by section; scripts whole (they document themselves in comments). Files under a folder named incidents/ or cases/ rank above general docs - keep one short file per solved problem there (symptom, cause, how it was found, fix) and Lanxang starts from it next time. Automatic attachment exists because small local models often skip optional lookups.

docs.title: jellyfin
docs.text: Field Default Description enabled false Offer get_jellyfin_sessions / get_jellyfin_activity / get_jellyfin_plugins to chat. url http://jellyfin:8096 Jellyfin base URL as reachable from Lanxang. api_key "" A Jellyfin API key (Dashboard > API Keys) created for Lanxang.

docs.title: health
docs.text: Field Default Description status_urls {} name: url of JSON status feeds that get_host_health includes (e.g. a RAID-card watchdog). storage_paths {} label: path whose disk usage the web home page's Storage & RAID card shows - e.g. media array: /media with the array bind-mounted read-only into the container. Software-RAID (/proc/mdstat) and Proxmox ZFS pools are shown automatically. alerts true Host health alerts (below) temp_margin_c 5.0 Alert when a sensor is this close to its own "high" limit, two samples in a row memory_percent 90 Alert when memory use reaches this disk_percent 90 Alert when the root disk or any storage_paths entry reaches this disk_hot_hdd_c 55 Proxmox disk health: a spinning disk this hot (°C) at two scans in a row disk_hot_ssd_c 70 The same for SSDs and NVMe drives disk_life_percent 10 Alert when an SSD has this much of its life left, or less

docs.title: Host health alerts
docs.text:
Every atlas-scan pass (lanxang sample) checks the machine lanxang runs on and sends one alert when a problem starts and another when it clears:

  • a temperature sensor within temp_margin_c of the limit the chip itself reports (CPUs and NVMe drives report one; sensors without a limit are skipped);
  • memory, the root disk or a storage_paths disk above its limit;
  • a container that crashed (stopped with an error code), keeps restarting, or fails its health check;
  • a status_urls feed whose state is anything but ok (for example a RAID-card watchdog saying warn).

Containers that sleep on purpose are not problems. One that stopped cleanly (exit code 0), such as a game room an idle timer shuts down, shows as Asleep on the home page and never alerts. For an app that sleeps but exits with an error code, add the label lanxang.on-demand=true (the older atlas.on-demand=true still works). The /api/summary tile data counts them as containers_asleep.

docs.title: Disk health (Proxmox)
docs.text:
With Proxmox set up, every lanxang proxmox scan (every 15 minutes in atlas-scan) also reads each node's disks: the SMART result, how much life an SSD has left, its temperature and its bad-sector count (reallocated, pending and uncorrectable sectors; media errors on NVMe). Home's Storage & RAID card gets one line per node (13 disks · all healthy · warmest 48°C · lowest life left 92%) and a line for each disk with a problem. One alert when a disk fails its SMART check, runs hot, or is nearly worn out, and one when that clears. Bad sectors alert each time the count goes up; a disk that has carried a few for years without change is fine. Needs nothing beyond the PVEAuditor token.

A status feed only reachable from Docker's network can be read as a file instead: mount its directory read-only and use a file:// URL (raid card: file:///run/raid-watchdog/status.json).

docs.title: access
docs.text:
Who reaches the public services and from where (web /access). lanxang access collect (run by atlas-scan each cycle) reads new Traefik access-log lines and app sign-ins, and geolocates IPs locally with DB-IP's free City Lite database (CC BY 4.0, downloaded monthly) plus the posture ASN table - no visitor IP leaves the host.

Field Default Description enabled false Turn collection on traefik_log /traefik-logs/access.log Traefik access log (mount it read-only into atlas-scan) geo_path inventory/dbip-city-lite.mmdb Where the monthly geo database is kept jellyfin_url / jellyfin_api_key "" Read sign-ins and failed attempts from Jellyfin's activity log home_ips [] Your WAN IPs - shown as "home", not drawn on the map ignore_ips [] IPs to skip entirely (e.g. an uptime checker) retention_days 30 Older hits, sign-ins and IPs are deleted

docs.title: map
docs.text:
hosts lists other machines to draw on the network map (lanxang map, web /map). Lanxang only checks their TCP reachability - it never acts on them.

Field Default Description name (required) Label on the map address (required) IP or hostname role "" Short description ports [22] TCP ports to test (a machine is "up" if any accepts)

A host whose address equals proxmox.host gets the Proxmox guests drawn under it; the one serving intelligence.ollama_host is labelled as the AI endpoint.

docs.title: scan
docs.text:
Controls lanxang scan, whole-LAN device discovery. Sightings link into the device inventory shown by lanxang devices (see CLI Reference).

Field Default Description enabled true Must be true for lanxang scan to run subnets [] CIDR subnets to scan; empty = the default-route interface's own networks timeout 0.5 Per-address TCP connect timeout, in seconds discover true Ask devices their own name and model over mDNS/Bonjour and SSDP/UPnP (a few seconds per scan); shown as clues for new devices

How often the atlas-scan container loops lanxang scan; lanxang discover; lanxang proxmox scan; lanxang map is controlled by the LANXANG_SCAN_MINUTES environment variable (docker-compose.yml), default 15 - not a lanxang.yaml field, since it's a property of the compose service's loop, not of scanning itself.

lanxang scan never pings and never opens a raw socket: it TCP-connects to port 9 on every address in scope, which makes the kernel ARP-resolve each live host, then reads /proc/net/arp for the resulting IP-to-MAC table (only complete entries count — an address nobody answered for isn't in it) and does a best-effort reverse DNS lookup for a hostname. This needs host networking (network_mode: host) but no extra capabilities. With discover on it also sends one mDNS question and one SSDP search to the LAN and reads each answering UPnP device's own description - read-only, and nothing leaves the network. The maker of each MAC address comes from the IEEE's public list (inventory/oui.csv, downloaded monthly; without internet it is skipped). A scan refuses to run over more than 1024 addresses at once — narrow subnets if your LAN is bigger than that.

docs.title: Weekly summary
docs.text: Every Sunday from 18:00 (in notify.timezone; UTC when empty) the next lanxang scan sends one message on how the week went: internet outages, services below 100%, new devices and how many wait for a name, open alerts, heartbeats, disks and the UPS - only the parts you use. Getting it also tells you lanxang itself is alive. notify.weekly_summary: false turns it off; quiet hours over Sunday evening hold it.

docs.title: Daily summary
docs.text:
Set notify.daily_summary to a time ("08:00", 24 h, in notify.timezone - the alert time zone, not the display one; UTC when empty) and the first lanxang scan after it sends one message on what changed in the last 24 hours: the Activity page's "What changed" items (new devices, alerts that started or cleared, Proxmox and container changes), public routes added or removed since the snapshot a day earlier, and known devices that went quiet. A day with nothing to tell sends nothing. Empty (the default) is off; the Setup page's Daily summary card sets it. Quiet hours and Pause alerts hold it until the next scan after they end. A time close to midnight (say "23:55") is skipped on a day when no scan runs between it and midnight, so pick one at least one scan interval before midnight. After the summary has been off for more than two days, the next one doesn't list devices as "gone quiet" (it can't tell which ones went quiet yesterday); it starts tracking again from that day.

notify:
  timezone: America/Detroit
  daily_summary: "08:00"

docs.title: Quiet hours
docs.text:
A weekly schedule when no alert messages go out - the night, or the Sunday update window. Problems still show on the Alerts page; only the messages are held, the same as Pause alerts. Add them on the Alerts page (times in your browser's time zone, which is saved as notify.timezone) or in lanxang.yaml:

notify:
  timezone: America/Detroit       # an IANA name; UTC when empty
  quiet_hours:
    - {start: "23:00", end: "07:00"}                 # every night (ends next morning)
    - {start: "03:00", end: "06:00", days: [sun]}     # Sunday updates

A window that ends before it starts runs over midnight and belongs to the day it starts. A schedule lanxang can't read never silences anything.

docs.title: display
docs.text:
How times read everywhere: every web page, alert messages, the test alert and the weekly summary. Usually set from the web UI (Preferences > Time & date, saved to inventory/settings.yaml); a value set here wins.

display:
  clock: 24h               # or 12h
  time_zone: browser       # browser (each viewer's own), UTC, or an IANA name like America/New_York
  date_format: iso         # iso 2026-11-19, dmy 19/11/2026, mdy 11/19/2026

With browser, pages show each viewer's own time zone; messages have no viewer, so they use UTC and say so.

Home's Since you were here remembers your last visit in a lanxang-seen cookie: two times in UTC (when the current visit's window starts and when you last loaded Home), nothing else. Lanxang sets it on each Home load (HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, kept a year); it is read only by your own Lanxang server and never sent anywhere else. A visit ends after 30 minutes away; without the cookie Home shows the last 24 hours, and never more than 7 days. Home reads No recent scan when the newest scan is older than three scan intervals (LANXANG_SCAN_MINUTES, see scan); set it in .env so the web container sees the same value as atlas-scan.

docs.title: Prometheus metrics
docs.text:
/metrics serves what lanxang already knows in Prometheus format, for Grafana or any Prometheus-compatible scraper: uptime checks (including Internet, Router and DNS) and their response times, device counts by state, open alerts, disk temperature / SMART / life left (Proxmox, TrueNAS, Synology), UPS charge and battery state, heartbeats, and Pi-hole / AdGuard Home totals. Nothing is measured on request; a source that isn't set up is left out. Sign in, or send the read-only API token (lanxang auth token) as a Bearer token:

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: lanxang
    scrape_interval: 60s
    authorization: {credentials: <lanxang auth token>}
    static_configs: [{targets: ["atlas.example:8420"]}]

docs.title: Alerts page
docs.text:
The web page's Alerts tab lists everything the checks below find: Needs action (problems: these also go to every notify: channel), Watching (shown on the page only) and Resolved in the last 7 days. Each item links to the page where you can investigate it, and resolves by itself once the check no longer sees it. One-off findings, such as a newly opened port, stay under Needs action for 7 days. Resolved items are kept for 30 days.

  • Acknowledge: you've seen it. It moves down the list and off the Home page; a one-off finding is cleared.
  • Mute this alert / this device (1 day, 7 days or always): no more messages about it - when the alert is about a device, about anything on that device - but it stays listed. Muted at the top of the page lists them, each with Unmute.
  • Pause alerts (1 hour, 4 hours or a day) for maintenance: nothing is sent, problems are still recorded, and a banner shows until Resume now or the time runs out.

One alert per outage. When a switch or access point on the cabling map goes offline, the offline devices wired behind it fold under it: one alert ("core-switch is offline - 12 devices behind it unreachable") and one message, instead of one per device. Only the topmost offline box counts, so a dead core switch doesn't also report the edge switch behind it. Switches and APs are matched to inventory devices by MAC, then IP; muting the switch mutes its outage. Without a cabling map, every important device alerts on its own as before.

docs.title: wiring
docs.text:
The cabling map (web /cabling): every switch port, what's plugged into it, patch panels, and cable health. Read-only: lanxang reads your switches over SNMPv3 and, optionally, a UniFi console, and never changes their settings. The atlas-scan container refreshes it every cycle; the page's Refresh map button does it on demand.

wiring:
  enabled: true
  switches:
    - name: core-switch          # secrets in .env: LANXANG_SNMP_CORE_SWITCH_AUTH / _PRIV
      host: 192.168.1.2
      priv: aes                  # des only for old gear that offers nothing else
    - name: nas                  # SNMPv2c: read-only community in .env as LANXANG_SNMP_NAS_COMMUNITY
      host: 192.168.1.20
      version: 2c
  unifi:
    enabled: true                # a local View Only account: LANXANG_UNIFI_USER / LANXANG_UNIFI_PASS in .env
    url: https://192.168.1.1
Field Default Description switches [] Switches, routers and NAS boxes that speak the standard MIBs (IF-MIB, LLDP-MIB, BRIDGE-MIB). version: "3" (default, authPriv; snmp_user defaults to lanxang) or "2c" with a read-only community - unencrypted, so only when the device offers nothing else. See Supported hardware unifi off Adds UniFi gateway/AP/switch ports and their uplinks, which SNMP can't see cabling_file cabling.yaml Patch panels and wall jacks, by hand (see cabling.example.yaml) not_managed [] Addresses never suggested for a login (the Setup tab's Don't ask adds them) keep_snapshots 30 Scans kept for "changes since the last scan" and cable health history timeout 10 Seconds per SNMP or UniFi request

docs.title: Traffic
docs.text: Each scan compares every port's byte counters (64-bit ifHCInOctets/ifHCOutOctets over SNMP; UniFi's port table) with the scan before, giving the average traffic over that gap - 15 minutes with the default scan interval, so short bursts are smoothed out. Nothing extra is polled. On the map, a cable over half its link speed is drawn thick orange and over 80% red, and its label shows the rate. The Port map has a Traffic (24 h) column with a small graph per port; hover it for now, in/out and the peak. Rates are kept 7 days. A counter reset (switch reboot) skips one point instead of showing a spike.

docs.title: Cable health
docs.text:
Each scan compares every connected port's counters with the scan before it, so only new errors count. A switch reboot that resets the counters is recognised and ignored.

Finding Level What it usually means CRC / alignment errors growing (10 or more per scan, above 0.01% of packets; 0.1% = problem) watch → problem A damaged cable, a bad jack or a worn patch lead Half duplex, or late collisions problem Duplex mismatch: one end is set to a fixed speed Link slower than the port ran before (e.g. 100 Mbit/s instead of 1 Gbit/s) watch A damaged wire pair or bad jack, or simply a computer asleep Link went down and up since the last scan watch Unplugged, rebooted, or a loose connector Output errors growing watch Congestion or a failing port PoE fault: a powered device detected but not powered problem A bad cable, or the device needs more power than the port gives PoE budget 90% or more used watch Another powered device (camera, access point) may not start

Finding switches to add: lanxang notices network gear it can't read yet: devices that answer SNMPv3 discovery (the maker comes from the answer, e.g. Cisco, Netgear, MikroTik) and devices a mapped switch hears announcing themselves as a bridge, router or access point over LLDP. NAS and Linux SNMP agents are left out. The Cabling page then says how many devices could show their ports with a login, the device's own page links to the Setup tab with the address filled in, and the Switches card lists them under Found on your network with Use and Don't ask. Lanxang never tries passwords: you give the SNMPv3 login, press Test, then Save.

PoE: ports powering a device show ⚡ on the faceplate, ports that can supply PoE but aren't have a dashed outline, and each device's line shows its PoE use and budget ("PoE 6.5 W of 30 W"). Hover a port for the PoE class, mode and watts. Switches report this over SNMP (the standard POWER-ETHERNET-MIB; per-port watts only come from UniFi), UniFi devices through the console. "Started/stopped delivering PoE" appears with the other changes since the last scan.

Spanning tree, link bundles and VLANs: when two or more cables join the same two switches or routers, the map checks spanning tree. If all but one cable is blocked, the spare shows as a grey dotted standby line, with a quiet note saying which port is idle. If more than one cable carries traffic, that's a loop risk: a warning at the top of the page and one alert (plus another when it's fixed). Cables bundled with LACP draw thicker and are labelled with the bundle name (for example Po1), with no warning. Hover a port to see its bundle, spanning-tree state and VLANs ("VLAN 1, tagged 20, 30"). When the switches carry more than one VLAN, a VLAN picker above the faceplates dims every port not on the chosen VLAN. The switch model (from sysDescr) shows next to its name. All of this uses standard MIBs (BRIDGE-MIB spanning tree, IEEE 802.3ad LAG-MIB, Q-BRIDGE-MIB VLANs). UniFi devices report their spanning-tree state and bundles through the console. A switch that lacks one of these tables just shows nothing for it.

Problems turn the port red on the faceplate, appear in Cable health and send one alert to every notify: channel, plus another alert when they clear. "Watch" findings are shown on the page only, because they have harmless causes too often to send alerts about. Switches without the EtherLike counters fall back to plain input errors, and UniFi ports use the console's own error counts.

docs.title: uptime
docs.text:
Is each service you care about answering? Add checks on the web page (Servers → Uptime: name, address, Add; your public hostnames are offered as one-click suggestions) or here. The atlas-scan container tries every check once a minute.

uptime:
  fail_after: 2                 # failures in a row before a check counts as down
  checks:
    - name: Media server
      target: https://media.example.org     # up when it answers below HTTP 500 - a login page counts
    - name: NAS (SMB)
      target: 192.0.2.20:445                # up when the port accepts a connection
      timeout: 5                            # seconds, default 10

A check that fails fail_after times in a row is down: one alert ("Media server is down"), listed on the Alerts page, and one "back up" message saying how long it was down. Mute or pause it from the Alerts page like any other alert. The page shows each check's response time over 24 hours and its uptime over 24 hours, 7 days and 30 days; results are kept 30 days. Certificates aren't verified here - expiry and trust are the certificate watch's job (security.cert_watch). A list set in lanxang.yaml wins over the page and makes the page read-only.

docs.title: Heartbeats
docs.text:
For jobs lanxang can't check from outside, such as a nightly backup or a cron job: add one on Servers → Uptime (or under uptime.heartbeats), then have the job call its address when it finishes. Add /fail when it failed.

your-backup-command && curl -fsS -m 10 http://atlas.example:8420/ping/<token> \
                    || curl -fsS -m 10 http://atlas.example:8420/ping/<token>/fail

uptime:
  heartbeats:
    - name: Nightly backup
      every_minutes: 1440   # how often it runs
      grace_minutes: 60     # how late it may be

A heartbeat that hasn't pinged within every_minutes + grace_minutes is late: one alert, and one when it pings again. A /fail ping alerts within a minute. Nothing is said before the first ping. The address needs no sign-in (the token in it is the password), so if lanxang sits behind a sign-in proxy, ping it on its own network address. Renaming a heartbeat changes its address.

docs.title: internet
docs.text:
Internet health, checked with the uptime checks once a minute (lanxang uptime check, run by atlas-scan). Lanxang opens a TCP connection to each target and to your default gateway (the router); no ping, so no extra privileges. Results show on Servers → Uptime and as a tile on Home.

Key Default What it does enabled true false turns the check off targets ["1.1.1.1:443", "8.8.8.8:443", "9.9.9.9:443"] host:port to reach; the internet is up when any answers timeout 3.0 Seconds to wait for each dns_name example.com Looked up each minute to check name lookups work; "" turns that off dns_servers [] Ask these directly (your router, Pi-hole...), one row each; empty = this machine's own resolver speed_test false A daily speed test after 04:00 (notify.timezone), shown on Home; see below

Speed test: with speed_test: true, lanxang internet speed (run by atlas-scan every pass) measures download, upload and ping once a day, on the first pass after 04:00 local time so it doesn't slow anyone's evening. It uses Cloudflare's public speed test (speed.cloudflare.com), four streams at once, about 260 MB per run; nothing about you is sent. Home shows the last result and the slowest download of the past 30 days. There is no alert: one slow result usually means the line was busy, not broken. lanxang internet speed --force runs one now; so does Test on the Setup tab's Internet speed test card.

Name lookups (DNS): a working connection with a broken DNS server still means no websites. Lanxang looks up dns_name once a minute and shows it under Internet. After uptime.fail_after failed minutes in a row - while the internet itself answers - you get one alert, and one when lookups work again.

The internet counts as down after uptime.fail_after failed minutes in a row. The alert for the drop only arrives if your alert service works without the internet (ntfy on your own network, for example); the one when it's back always does, with how long it lasted. The outage list says whether the router kept answering - then the problem was on the provider's side.

docs.title: dns_filter
docs.text:
Pi-hole (version 6) or AdGuard Home, read with every lanxang scan (or lanxang dns check). Easiest from Setup → Pi-hole or AdGuard Home. Read-only: lanxang never changes blocking or lists.

Key Default What it does enabled false Turn the watch on kind pihole pihole or adguard url "" Its web address, e.g. http://192.168.1.53 user "" AdGuard Home's username (Pi-hole has none) verify_ssl false Check the certificate on an https:// address timeout 5.0 Seconds to wait

The password goes in the LANXANG_DNS_PASSWORD secret (Setup stores it for you). For Pi-hole, an app password (Settings → Web interface / API) works too and is the one to use with two-factor sign-in on. Lanxang signs out of Pi-hole after every read, so it never uses up Pi-hole's session slots. Ad blocking off at two checks in a row sends one alert, and one more when it's back on - a short pause doesn't.

docs.title: homeassistant
docs.text:
Home Assistant, read with every lanxang scan (and lanxang ha check) through its REST API. Set it up in Setup → Home Assistant. Off by default.

Field Default Description enabled false Turn it on url Home Assistant's address, like http://homeassistant.local:8123 verify_ssl false Check its certificate timeout 15 Seconds to wait offline_hours 6 A device counts as dropped out when all its sensors, cameras, locks, switches, lights... have been unavailable this long battery_percent 20 A battery at or under this is low

The long-lived access token (Home Assistant: your profile → Security → Long-lived access tokens) is the LANXANG_HA_TOKEN secret. Home shows a Smart home tile and card: devices that dropped out, low batteries and updates waiting. TVs, media players, remotes and phones are left out of "dropped out" - they go unavailable whenever they're switched off. Alerts: Home Assistant not answering (two checks in a row), a device dropping out, a low battery - once each, and once when it's fine again. Updates are listed to watch, never messaged.

docs.title: nas
docs.text:
TrueNAS or Synology disk and pool health, read with every lanxang scan (and lanxang nas check). Set it up in Setup → TrueNAS or Synology. Off by default.

Field Default Description enabled false Turn it on kind truenas truenas or synology url The web address: https://192.0.2.20 (TrueNAS, https only), https://192.0.2.20:5001 (Synology) user TrueNAS: the user the API key belongs to. Synology: the account lanxang signs in with name What to call it on Home and in alerts; the address's host name when empty verify_ssl false Check its certificate (leave off for the usual self-signed one) timeout 10 Seconds to wait

The API key (TrueNAS) or password (Synology) is the LANXANG_NAS_PASSWORD secret.

  • TrueNAS (24.10 and newer) is read over its JSON-RPC websocket API, the one that replaces the REST API TrueNAS is removing. Make an API key for a user with the read-only admin role. lanxang only uses https: TrueNAS revokes a key sent without encryption.
  • Synology (DSM 7): DSM only lets administrators read storage, so make an admin account for lanxang, deny it every shared folder and application, and leave two-factor off for it. lanxang signs out after every read.

Home's Storage & RAID card shows each pool or volume (health, how full) and the disks the same way as Proxmox ones (see Disk health under health). Alerts: one when a pool or volume isn't healthy and one when it is again; disk alerts use the same health.disk_* limits. Built from the vendors' API documentation and not yet checked against real hardware - if something reads wrong on yours, please open an issue.

docs.title: ups
docs.text:
Alerts on a power cut, a low battery, and when power is back, read from a NUT server (Network UPS Tools, TCP 3493). The computer the UPS's USB cable goes into usually runs one: nut-server on Linux, or the network UPS server option on Synology, QNAP, Unraid and TrueNAS (add lanxang's address to its allowed list). Set it up on Setup → UPS or here. atlas-scan reads it once a minute; only LIST commands are sent, so no login is needed.

ups:
  enabled: true
  host: 192.168.1.20
  port: 3493
  name: ""          # blank = every UPS that server lists (Synology calls its UPS "ups")

The UPS status (charge, time left on battery, load) is shown at the top of Servers → Uptime. If the server can't be read, the last known state is kept and the Alerts page shows it under Watching - a hiccup reading it never counts as a power change.

docs.title: security
docs.text:
LAN watch: lanxang lan check looks for a second DHCP server and for something impersonating your router. atlas-scan runs it after every device scan, and the result shows as the LAN tile on the Security tab (Exposure).

security:
  dhcp_servers: [192.168.1.5]   # only if something besides the router hands out addresses (Pi-hole, a second router)
Field Default Description dhcp_probe true Send one DHCP discover per run and list every server that answers. It never asks for or takes an address dhcp_timeout 3.0 Seconds to wait for answers dhcp_servers [] DHCP servers you expect besides the default gateway port_watch true lanxang ports check: alert on newly open ports (below) snmp_discovery true During lanxang ports check, send each device online the standard SNMPv3 discovery message (no user name, no password, so never a failed login) to find switches and routers that could show their ports port_timeout 0.5 Seconds per port connect extra_ports [] Ports to watch besides the ~25 common service ports Finding Level What it usually means A DHCP server that is neither the gateway nor listed problem A router plugged in backwards, a VM or container running DHCP by mistake, or an attacker handing out their own gateway No DHCP server answered two runs in a row (after answering before) problem DHCP is down: new devices and renewing ones can't get an address No DHCP server has ever answered watch Usually this host's firewall dropping the answers: allow incoming UDP port 68 (on firewalld: firewall-cmd --add-port=68/udp --permanent, then --reload) The gateway's IP answers from a different MAC than the one learned on the first run problem ARP spoofing (a man in the middle), or you replaced the router: run lanxang lan check --trust-gateway to accept the new MAC A wired UniFi client using the gateway's IP problem Something claiming to be the router (needs wiring.unifi) The gateway's MAC also answers for another address watch Usually harmless (proxy ARP, a router with two addresses) One IP on two wired UniFi clients watch An address conflict, or a recent DHCP reassignment

Problems send one alert to every notify: channel and another when they clear. The ARP checks see what the lanxang host sees; UniFi's client list (when wiring.unifi is set) widens that to the rest of the wired network. Hearing DHCP answers needs UDP port 68: the Docker image ships lanxang-dhcp-python, an interpreter copy holding only that one permission. Run outside Docker as a normal user, the probe reports that it can't listen and the ARP checks still run.

docs.title: Open-port watch
docs.text:
lanxang ports check (run by atlas-scan after every device scan) looks at three things, all read-only:

  • LAN devices: a plain TCP connect to about 25 common service ports (SSH, telnet, web, file sharing, remote desktop, VNC, databases, camera streams, MQTT, printers) on every device that is online, within your scan subnets. It never sends data or logs in.
  • This host: sockets listening for other machines (loopback-only ones are left out).
  • The router: port forwards and the UPnP switch from the UniFi console when wiring.unifi is set, and the standard UPnP port-mapping list that most home routers answer (only the default gateway is asked).

The first run learns what is normal and sends nothing. After that every newly open port sends one alert (risky ones such as telnet, SMB, remote desktop or databases say so), a new port forward or UPnP mapping alerts as "opened to the internet", and UPnP being switched on alerts. A port that closes and opens again later doesn't alert twice. Each device's page lists its open ports; the Security tab (Exposure)'s Public exposure tab shows the router's forwards, UPnP and the latest new ports.

docs.title: Certificate watch
docs.text:
lanxang certs check (run by atlas-scan, but only once a day) opens a TLS connection to every hostname in your Traefik routes, plus any you list, the same way a browser would, and reads each certificate's expiry date. Nothing is changed and no login is needed. Behind Cloudflare (or any proxy) that is the certificate visitors actually get.

security:
  cert_watch: true          # false turns it off
  cert_hosts: []            # more hostnames to check, e.g. a router or NAS with its own certificate
  cert_warn_days: 14        # first alert
  cert_urgent_days: 3       # second, red alert (also sent once it has expired)
  cert_timeout: 5.0

One alert per hostname each time things get worse (14 days left, then 3 days or expired), one when a browser would refuse the certificate (wrong name, untrusted issuer), and a "Resolved" once it is renewed. A hostname that can't be reached is only shown, not alerted: outages are the health checks' job. The Posture page's Public exposure tab shows days left next to each route, yellow inside the warning window and red when urgent or untrusted. lanxang certs check --force checks right away.

docs.title: Internet view
docs.text:
lanxang internet check (run by atlas-scan, but only once a day, or sooner when your public IP changes) asks Shodan's free InternetDB what it last saw on your home's public IP: open ports and any CVEs it reports for that IP. The IP is the one posture collection already reads, so posture.enabled must be on. No account or key is needed.

Privacy: this sends your home IP to Shodan once a day, so it is off until you turn it on (here, or on the Setup page's Internet view card).

posture:
  internet_view: true       # off by default
  expected_ports: [80, 443] # open ports that don't alert (port numbers, any protocol)
  internet_view_url: https://internetdb.shodan.io/{ip}

Each open port that isn't in expected_ports raises one alert ("Port 22 is open to the internet"), cleared with one more message when Shodan no longer sees it or when you add the port to expected_ports (saving the Setup card rechecks the last answer straight away, without asking Shodan again); each reported CVE raises one alert too. The Security page's Public exposure tab shows What the internet sees: each port marked expected or not, the CVEs, the software Shodan detected, and when Shodan was last asked. This is Shodan's last scan, not a live test: a port you just closed can still show for a while. A failed lookup keeps the last answer and the open alerts, and so does an empty answer from Shodan after it had data for your IP (shown as "Shodan has no current data for this IP"); a failed lookup is tried again an hour later rather than the next day. A new public IP starts from nothing. lanxang internet check --force looks up right away.

docs.title: notify
docs.text:
Where alerts go: new devices, important devices gone offline, VPN/torrent clients disconnected, and sign-ins from new places. Set any number of channels — every one that is set gets each alert, and one failing never stops the others. Check your setup with lanxang notify test.

notify:
  ntfy:                              # free phone app (ntfy.sh, or your own server)
    url: https://ntfy.sh
    topic: my-homelab-a8f3k2         # pick something hard to guess on the public server
  webhooks:                          # Discord / Slack webhook URLs, or any URL that takes JSON
    - https://discord.com/api/webhooks/123/abc
    - http://homeassistant.local:8123/api/webhook/lanxang
  email:
    host: smtp.example.com
    port: 587
    user: atlas@example.com
    to: [me@example.com]
  apprise:                           # 100+ more services, see the Apprise wiki
    - tgram://bottoken/ChatID
  signal:                            # signal-cli-rest-api
    url: http://signal-cli:8080
    number: "+15551234567"
    recipients: ["+15559876543"]
Channel Fields Notes ntfy url, topic, token Markdown messages with a title. token (or LANXANG_NTFY_TOKEN in .env) for a protected server webhooks list of URLs discord.com/api/webhooks/... and hooks.slack.com/... get their own format; any other URL gets {"title", "text", "source": "lanxang"} as JSON email host, port (587), starttls (true), user, password, sender, to Port 465 uses implicit TLS. Put the password in .env as LANXANG_SMTP_PASSWORD rather than here apprise list of Apprise URLs Telegram, Pushover, Gotify, Matrix, Teams and more. Needs the apprise package — the Docker image has it; with pip, pip install "lanxang[alerts]" signal url, number, recipients Through signal-cli-rest-api. recipients can be numbers or group IDs

Beside the channels: timezone (the alert time zone, an IANA name; UTC when empty) for quiet_hours and the summaries, weekly_summary (true) and daily_summary ("HH:MM", empty = off) - see Weekly summary and Daily summary.

An alert counts as delivered when at least one channel took it; if every channel fails it stays queued and is retried on the next run.

The first successful run of each source (lan, proxmox, ...) is a baseline — it never generates new-device alerts by itself. After that, new-device alerts roll up: if one was already sent in the last 24 hours, further new devices are held and folded into the next message instead of each firing its own alert. An important device going quiet (missed the last 2 successful runs of every source) alerts once per episode, not on every scan it stays quiet.

docs.title: Supported hardware
docs.text:
Lanxang works on any home network with no logins at all: it finds every device from its own LAN scan, watches for rogue DHCP servers and spoofed gateways, lists open ports, checks your public certificates, and runs uptime checks. Connecting your gear adds detail - switch ports, Wi-Fi access points, VMs. Everything lanxang reads is read-only, and it never changes a device's settings.

On the Setup tab, What's on your network? asks what you have and shows only the matching cards. Gear lanxang has already found is ticked for you.

docs.title: What works today
docs.text:
You have How lanxang reads it What it adds Set up on Any router (ISP box, ASUS, Netgear, eero, Fritz!Box, Deco...) Nothing to connect Devices, DHCP/ARP watch, open ports, router port forwards via UPnP where it's on - Managed switch (Cisco SG/CBS, Netgear Smart, TP-Link JetStream, Zyxel GS1900, Aruba Instant On, MikroTik...)
